claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by competition between the oxidation kinetics of passivating and non-passivating elements.
Cr is a high-redox-potential, passivating alloying element.
Increasing Cr or other passivating-element concentrations enhances formation of a coherent protective oxide scale.
A coherent protective oxide scale slows further oxidation and preserves material integrity.
The initial material is an as-synthesized multiprincipal-element alloy containing passivating elements such as Cr and other alloying elements.
Cr concentration will be varied upward and downward while the other alloying components are kept constant.
Samples will be exposed to oxidizing environments at 800–1200 °C for sustained durations.
Oxide-scale nature, continuity, and uniformity mediate oxidation behavior.
Cr2O3 is an example of the oxide scale expected to form on the alloy surface.
Changing passivating-element concentration alters local redox potential and thereby directs competition among oxide phases.
Higher passivating-element concentrations preferentially promote a coherent, slow-growing, passivating oxide.
Lower passivating-element concentrations produce non-uniform and less-protective oxide structures.
Increasing passivating-species concentration will reduce oxidation kinetics relative to the baseline alloy.
Increasing passivating-species concentration will produce a more uniform and protective oxide layer relative to the baseline alloy.
Increasing passivating-species concentration will improve retention of material integrity relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy has known oxidation kinetics and oxide-scale morphology under the specified conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold from 800 to 1200 °C during prolonged oxidizing exposure.
Applicability may differ outside 800–1200 °C or under different oxidative stressors.
A controlled baseline-versus-increased-passivating-element comparison can be evaluated through weight gain, scale thickness, oxide morphology and composition, and phase identification.
Failure of the increased-passivating-element alloy to show a statistically significant improvement over the baseline under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
